en: Preface to the *General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* The *General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* consists of the concluding remarks of the Master Daxu of Guangling as he expounded upon the sutra.
What is termed its "general meaning" describes the fundamental intention of all Buddhas, reveals the wondrous nature of sentient beings, and harmonizes the partial with the perfect.

This is consistent. It clarifies the general path of the school’s teachings. It is because of the causal conditions for the one great matter that the ignorant and small-minded are unable to suddenly realize it;

because the true mark of all phenomena is so profound and subtle that it is difficult to proclaim in words. Thus, when the Great Awakened One was first born, he immediately revealed his true mechanism through a mere gesture;
later, at the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, he fully manifested his wondrous essence from the white tuft between his brows. Those with dim eyes find it difficult to peer into; its auspicious...

How could such principles be hidden? Thus, those who open up expedient means within the Ninefold Canon and reveal true wisdom within the Three Vehicles do so specifically because the true sound is distant and vast, and they have not yet encountered those whose faculties are ready.
As for the secret pivot being silently communicated and the profound axis being wondrously harmonized, every subtle teaching and indirect guidance is nothing other than supreme practice.
Mundane conditions and the realms of lands are equal to the single wondrous mind; therefore, when one raises a hand—
Bowing his head, he was uniformly granted the seal of approval. It is like a great capital city: once one enters through any single gate, all eight thoroughfares become accessible.
Only you, Master, have not lost sight of the jewel within your robes and have personally ascended to the treasure-store.

Having expounded the meaning to illuminate the golden texts, you further investigated the mind and wielded the *cintāmaṇi*. You wrested wondrous understanding from the realm of discursive thought and penetrated the profound essence.
Prior to the era of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, the grasping at self was already forgotten and the wondrous perfection responded accordingly.

Thus, by raising a finger, the door of the stupa was opened and the entire body of the ancient Buddha was suddenly beheld; by observing the dragon girl’s offering of pearls, she swiftly departed for the Stainless World (*Vimalā*).

The realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were not separated from one another, and kalpas as vast as dust motes and ink were not distant. Entering the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, he sat upon the Inconceivable [Lotus Throne].
Discourse on the Site of Enlightenment: The single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed. These words are indeed free from falsehood.
Written with reverence by the Śramaṇa Faju of Tiantai, in the first month of winter in the year of Jiajing Dingyi, as a preface to the Opening of the Sūtra and the General Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra.
Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the ultimate realization of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the true practice of all Bodhisattvas.
It is that which the sentient beings of the six realms are deluded about, and it is the profound slander of the sons who do not recognize it.
Yet, regarding this slander, delusion, practice, and realization, there are four distinctions; whereas its source, essence, nature, and principle are without these four.
They are not one, yet because each of the four is identical, when a sage is born in the East, his Way is the same, his substance is the same, and his conduct—
whether in action or withdrawal, in teaching or transforming, even down to the most minute details of his deeds— is in every way the same as those in the South and North.

Throughout the upper, lower, and middle regions, extending to the entirety of the realms of existence and non-existence, there are holy beings born. Their paths are the same; their essence is the same;
and in their conduct, whether acting or withdrawing, in their teaching and transformation, and in every minute detail of their deeds, there is nothing that is not the same.
Because these four differ, heterodoxies have emerged in ancient times; their words are not uniform, their likes and dislikes are not uniform, and they even experience anxiety, distress, and fear.
Anger, joy, taking, and rejecting are all inconsistent. In the present age and the future, throughout all generations and amidst ten thousand changes, heterodox views will emerge;
their words will not be uniform, and their likes and dislikes will not be uniform. Even to the point of anxiety, suffering, fear, anger, joy, taking, and rejecting—all these will be inconsistent.
Because they are inconsistent, the ruts of chariots will differ and the characters of books will differ. How can there be a Great [Way]?
The Way does not give rise to slander, yet it is met with profound doubt; thus, it is not difficult for those who have first awakened, but it is difficult for those who learn later.
This is because they are fundamentally the same. Heaven constantly covers all equally, and Earth constantly supports all equally; it has never been that the Great Way does not proceed in common.
Thus, it is not difficult for those who learn later, but it is difficult for those who have first awakened. Because it is difficult for those who have first awakened, the one who has first awakened—
Mingdao practiced asceticism with such rigor as the six years at Mount Xue and the nine years at Shaolin.
He wandered restlessly like a dog that has lost its home and sought with urgent desperation like a deer parched with thirst. At times he resolved others' delusions by composing treatises;
at times he washed away others' errors by submitting petitions. For the sake of the Way, he was willing to sacrifice his body or forfeit his head. Or he engaged in great debate.
Yet [the Buddha’s] teachings comprise ten thousand words, yet there may be those so profound and obscure that not a single phrase is grasped.
One might go so far as to treat them like a slave, a dog, a blade of grass, or a mustard seed, all because a single word is not understood.

One might even go to the extreme of being cut, butchered, imprisoned, or boiled, for the sake of learning a half-verse. Alas! This is precisely why it is so difficult to attain initial awakening. It is not... [that it is easy].
It is difficult for later scholars. Thus, for those who study in later times, there are the scriptures of the Great Sage, as brilliant as the sun;

there are the commentaries of the Great Worthies, as luminous as the stars; there are the sublime treatises of eminent monks that resolve doubts; and there are the grand dialectics of the Great Masters that shatter uncertainty.

They point out the path for entering the Way with the precision of a bowstring; they open the great gate to realizing one's nature with the expansiveness of a wide vista. If one is willing to believe—

Attaining Buddhahood directly beneath one’s feet, all shall dwell in the world of stainless purity. If one is willing to practice, they will transcend the mundane and immediately surpass the ordinary, realizing the pure *dharmakāya*.
How much more so for those who have long since inherited the power of past roots of goodness and now encounter this Great Enlightenment:
where carriages share the same tracks and scripts share the same characters; where Heaven covers us equally and Earth sustains us alike; and where heterodox paths have ceased.

The Great Way is luminous. When slander and defilement are dispelled, the holy teaching becomes manifest. To clarify this very luminosity: look at the palm of your hand while the sun is at its zenith;
if you are willing to enter, you enter immediately. At home, you bow to your father and mother—what difficulty or peril could there be?

It is simply that you are unwilling to enter; yet it is truly easy and not difficult. It is simply that you are unwilling to believe. If you believe today, you enter the realm of the Buddha today. I say: No.
For those who study later, this is difficult; I am by nature truly dull and ignorant. Fortunately, I have entered the chamber of sincerity and clarity.

My learning is indeed shallow and narrow, yet like one encountering a teacher of awakening in a time of drought. Having been honored by the venerable assembly with this commission to propagate it, how could I dare not exhaust my heart in its exposition?
I humbly beseech the venerable assembly to keep in mind the intention of our Buddha, the Great Sage, that the True Dharma may long endure, and each of you—
One should conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find. Indeed, a hundred years pass like a flash of lightning. Among all things, humans are the most sentient;

yet if a person does not clarify this Way, after a hundred years, even if they wish for a human body, how could it be obtained? As for the principle of successive births, heaven and earth certainly have no time of cessation.
To surely obtain a human body, one fears that the forces of creation cannot provide exclusive control. May all people therefore take heed.
With single-minded dedication, I offer this verse of praise: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in seven fascicles— If this mind is momentarily distracted, it becomes difficult to clarify.
Love and hate, acceptance and rejection, and a thousand discriminations; Self and other, right and wrong, and ten thousand injustices.
The great ocean was never an obstacle to fish; The vast sky has always allowed cranes to soar and cry. This morning, I have met with this true teaching of Suchness; I only pray that you...

That which brings all things into being with supreme spiritual power is called "mystery" (miao). That which presides over all things without variation is called the "Dharma" (fa).
The Dharma is the nature (xing); mystery is the mind (xin). Indeed, this mind is inherently possessed by every person, and this nature is likewise inherently possessed by every person.
However, as for the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person, it is not that there is any difference in this mind or this nature; rather, it is...

It is merely that people differ in their realization of delusion. As for the fundamental substance of the mind-nature, there is originally no separation whatsoever between the sage and the ordinary person.

Not only are there no gaps between the sage and the ordinary person, but even from the heavens above to the earth below, throughout the myriad phenomena in their diversity, and within all movement and stillness, as well as every action and deed, there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation. Such being the case, the wondrous Dharma is...

This is an alternative name for the nature of the mind. The nature of the mind is one body with the Great Ultimate (*taiji*); it is fully present in both humans and things, and all beings, whether ordinary or sagely, share the same source.
What cause for doubt could there be? As for the lotus flower: it is pure and unstained, continuous and without interruption.

It also serves as a metaphor for this mind, which is uninterrupted between past and present, connecting the three periods of time; and which is without interval between form and emptiness, connecting the ten directions. Indeed...

The wondrous mind and wondrous nature of human beings have no beginning in the past and no end in the future; they are so vast that nothing exists outside them, and so subtle that nothing exists within them.
The *sūtra* is the direct discourse proclaimed by our Buddha, the Great Sage, to reveal this mind and this nature.
Because these words directly reveal the profound principle of the human heart, they are called a *sūtra*. Fascicle One.
This sutra consists of seven fascicles in total; this is the first, hence it is called "the first. The second through the seventh may be understood accordingly.
Although this sutra comprises but seven rolls, it in truth encompasses the Great Way of the three worlds and four dharma-realms.
This is because I have honored the command of the assembly to proclaim this sutra; however, my own talents are meager and my insight shallow.

Yao Qin (the Yao-Qin dynasty) was a "false king" of Eastern Jin; his surname was Yao and his name was Xing. He served as the sovereign of the Qin state. This sutra was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva, who received the imperial decree during the Yao-Qin period. Yao Qin... [is] Eastern Jin. [The text continues: ...This sutra is from the Qin...
The imperial decree commanded the translation [of the scriptures]; therefore, the name of the kingdom is recorded. "Tripiṭaka" (Sanzang) is a general title for a monk;

it refers to a monk who is proficient in the Sūtra-piṭaka, the Vinaya-piṭaka, and the Śāstra-piṭaka. "Dharmabhāṇaka" (Fashi) refers to one capable of propagating the teachings and worthy of serving as a model for humans and devas.
Kumārajīva is the name of a translated monk; this is rendered in Chinese as "Child Longevity" (Tongshou).

This refers to a monk who, though young in years, possesses the virtue of a venerable elder. "Translating by imperial decree" means that he submitted a memorial to the King regarding the translation of this sutra. raising an eyebrow falls into two or three [categories]. Even if one neither opens the mouth nor raises an eyebrow, one cannot avoid being scrutinized by the person of realization.

If it were otherwise, you should each look with your eyes before the mountain monk has opened his mouth, before you have reached the Dharma Hall, and before your parents had yet been born and heaven and earth had yet been divided. Look!
Look! What words and phrases could possibly express this wondrous Dharma? Heh! A clay ox carries the night to the lotus pond;
a wooden horse bears spring to the willow bank. Someone asked: "What is the meaning of 'a clay ox carrying the night to the lotus pond'?"
The Master said, "This is the meaning of arriving without having arrived. [The student] asked, "What is the meaning of 'A wooden horse carries spring to the willow bank'?
The Master said, "This is the meaning of coming without having come. [The student] said, "In that case, it is clearly at the head of the hundred grasses;
it is clearly the intent of the Patriarch. The Master said, "Furthermore, you do not understand how to translate this. [The student] asked, "How is it that one understands how to translate?"
The Master said, "Please listen to one verse from this mountain monk: In the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma there is not a single word;
From the beginning, the Three Baskets have misconstrued it. Today I shall once more firmly paste it back up; It is not like that fragrant flower emerging from the water at the time.

This is the sequential order. This chapter serves as the prelude to the *Miaojing* (The Wondrous Sutra). Regarding "the first":
this sutra consists of twenty-eight chapters, and as this is the opening chapter, it is designated as the first. Such an explanation is merely the interpretive understanding of the lecturers.

This subtle principle is called the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) in the *I Ching*; it is called principle (*li*) in heaven, earth, and the myriad things;
it is called the Way (*dao*) in the myriad transformations of creation; it is called the mind (*xin*) as the master of hatred and love, acceptance and rejection among humans and things;
and it is called nature (*xing*) as the awareness of movement and stillness, action and inaction, suffering and joy in the animate and the inanimate. Thus, it is both the Great Ultimate and the mind.
It is the nature; it is the principle. It is a single entity without duality.

"Square" means there are no four directions, eight corners, above, or below. That there are no four directions, eight corners, above, or below demonstrates the fundamental principle of the single ultimate as the unified whole.
That there is no prior limit, middle limit, or subsequent limit demonstrates the celestial mandate of the one Buddha as the total embodiment.

As for the other wondrous dharmas, one must, within stillness, sweep away all myriad distinctions and a thousand differences, as well as false cognitions and false views, and single-mindedly raise [the essential point].
This is the principle of being able to perceive. Ultimately, what is the fruit? At this point, there is a sudden awakening;
one must realize at once that which is called the Wondrous Dharma, the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*), the Principle, and the Nature of Mind—all of these are fully present within oneself.
How could they ever be lacking? Why then do you seek them outwardly? A question was asked: "The student simply accepts it directly."
[The student] asked, "Will I eventually attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Tell me what you have realized. What is it that you have realized?
He replied, "I have realized that I shall become a Buddha. The Master said, "That may well be so, but I fear it will result in a duality.
He asked, "What is the principle of undifferentiated wholeness? The Master said, "Clear wind through the bamboo by the two railings; bright moon over the pines in the courtyard."
"Thus have I heard. Regarding "thus have I heard," this is a conventional expression used across all the sūtras, meaning: "I personally heard this sūtra from the Buddha.
This was the formula employed by the Venerable Ānanda when compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, intended to indicate that this sūtra has a source of transmission.
One simply accepts it; there is nothing further to be said. Yet, as there is "is" and "is not," so too am I both real and delusory.
That which is the delusory self is precisely the physical form of each person’s four elements and six sense organs; to take this as the self is for the self to be unreal.
Since the self is unreal, hearing [the Dharma] also becomes delusory. As for the true self, the moment one directs the mind toward it, one is already mistaken; it is beyond movement.

When one thinks of it, it departs; yet in every dust mote it is not obscured, and it is ever-knowing with perfect clarity. There is no sound or fragrance to be heard or smelled, and no form or shape to be modeled or depicted.
It extends vertically through the three periods of time and pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions.
All Buddhas point to this true self as their nature; this is precisely what this sutra is. All Buddhas point to this true self and name it the Lamp; this is precisely what... [the sutra is].
This is the Dharma. By means of such a true and non-deceptive self, one listens to this true *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Then there is no dharma outside the mind, and no mind outside the dharmas. To speak of "mind," all dharmas are mind; even a lump of clay or a clod of earth [is so].
Husk, chaff, tiles, and rubble—all are one's own mind. To speak in terms of the Dharma, every moment of mind is the Dharma; joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure;
adversity, favor, grasping, and rejecting—all are the wondrous Dharma. Furthermore, that which is thus is what the sages call "nature.

When they speak of nature, there is nothing that does not accord with it. That which is not thus is what the multitude discusses as "sentiment. When they discuss sentiment, there is no mutual agreement.
It is because they are not identical. Thus, the six realms and four modes of birth, with their cycles of suffering and joy, ascent and descent, are fundamentally non-existent yet appear as real.
It is because they are identical that the myriad things are but a single horse—what is real and what is false? Heaven and earth are but a single finger.
Who is right and who is wrong? Only by understanding it in this way and harmonizing it in this way can it be called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
I have personally heard it from the Buddha; otherwise, the meaning of "Thus have I heard" would be as far apart as heaven and earth.

"The dragon follows [the clouds] and the wind follows the tiger; this is the Way of nature. Furthermore, it manifests that when a Great Sage appears and expounds the teachings, he is like the sun shining in the sky, such that among the myriad species there are none that do not behold him.
Moreover, taking the myriad species—whether far or near, high or low—it is shown that they all arrive [before him].
The Great Sage’s majestic virtue and benevolence are vast and complete; though unspoken, they are known, just as [the sun is known]."
The classical texts speak of how fame and reputation spread far and wide; among all those with breath and blood, there are none who do not revere and love them.
Indeed, from antiquity to the present, it has been because the Way and its Virtue (*dào-dé*) have not been clarified that one’s nature and destiny (*xìng-mìng*) remain unclarified.

If nature and destiny were clarified, then there would be nothing about the Way and its Virtue that remained unclarified. Nature is principle (*lǐ*); destiny is my own principle. As for this principle within me—
The principle regarding persons is clarified; as the principle regarding persons is clarified, the principle regarding things becomes even more clarified.

In this way, it extends to exhausting all categories of phenomenal existence and reaching the furthest reaches of the manifold world within the realm of emptiness, such that there is no principle that remains unclarified.

Since the principle is clarified, there is nothing about phenomena that remains unclarified. Since phenomena are clarified, that which is called morality, that which is called benevolence and righteousness, even ritual propriety, education, literature, and governance—all of these become clear.
Because the nature and mandate of the Great Sage are luminous, they are termed the Great Classic, the Great Root, the Great Dharma, the Great Way, the Great Virtue, and the Great Achievement.

Sound. Great Practice. Because he is fully endowed with myriad virtues, all those with breath—whether high or low, far or near—come to revere and love him as they would their own selves, loving themselves;
it requires no other teaching. He held up his *niwan* (wish-fulfilling jewel) and said: "Do you understand?"

If one were to encounter those who possess these characteristics within this assembly, there would be none who do not revere them; if one hears their words, there would be none who do not believe them;
if one follows their conduct, there would be none who are not delighted; and if one dwells together with them, there would be none who are not unified.
Should it be otherwise, let each person tie a "Ke" (克) character to their own liver and gallbladder. Thus, as they come and go, let them be driven by this "Ke" until it reaches its limit.
In the place where one may achieve mastery, one should spontaneously realize that throughout the ten directions all is benevolence and goodness.

Suddenly forgetting the mind of grasping and rejecting, one reaches the ultimate state of permanence across the three periods of time, perfectly entering the realm of true equanimity. When one arrives at such a moment, fame and reputation will overflow;
even the great and the small, the honored and the kin, will be matters within one's own sphere. What further cause for doubt could there be? He asked: "How so?"

This is precisely the meaning of "overcoming. The Master said, "It is like a neighbor building a wall; if it extends one foot beyond my house, you simply overcome that one foot so that it is as if it were never there at all.
[The student] asked, "If that is so, then making progress on the Path must be very easy indeed."
The Master said, "Though it is easy, people in the world are unwilling to overcome [their delusions]. [The student] asked, "When one is unwilling to overcome them, what then?
The Master said, "You are not right and I am wrong; now returns to the past. Tigers fight and dragons contend, never ceasing.
[The student] asked, "If one were to overcome them directly, what then? The Master said, "Heaven provides the timing; Earth provides the benefit. People and things are in harmony; the elders..."
Peaceful. The young hold it dear; friends trust it.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly (up to) as they gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
The essential purport of this section of the sutra is simply to provide the preface for the wondrous sutra; there is nothing else.
I have spoken. I, Shan-yeh, am not clever; let us once more examine this by means of the "Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Now, as for "immeasurable meanings": when one is in the state of vivid clarity, it is called the Mind; when it is the master of every dust mote and every world-system, it is called the Principle.
Our Ancestor, the Great Master Bodhidharma, came from the West and did not establish written words; he went directly...
Pointing directly to the human mind and seeing one’s nature to become a Buddha is called Chan.

The various masters of our own land, Confucius and Mencius, established their words and teachings to continue the way of the ancient sages and open the path for future learners; this is called the Middle Way (*zhongyong*).

Among those caught in the midst of worldly afflictions, those who do not understand this are called deluded and confused. Those who are intelligent enough to know this yet fail to practice it are said to be abandoning themselves. [There are] occasional...
There are those who understand this and yet practice it, but fail to reach this stage; they are called "lacking courage.

There are those who exert themselves with diligence day and night, yet ultimately achieve no genuine realization; they are called "lacking wisdom. There are those who attain the state of a minor sage or a divine immortal.
To be proficient in writing, eloquent in speech, skilled in the arts, and yet to remain stuck in the state of transformation—this is called "incomplete.
To have just attained thorough awakening and then immediately dwell in quiescent extinction—this is called "not great.

To divide this from that, clinging to the Way or clinging to Confucianism—this is called "not one. Furthermore, there are those who wear clothes and eat food, yet ultimately do not realize they are wearing clothes.
Who is it that eats? Furthermore, among those who know only wealth, honor, and splendor, who is it that does not know wealth, honor, and splendor?
Both are said to be unenlightened. [The Master] raised his *śakti* (ritual whisk) and asked, "Do you understand? If you can understand this," [then you have realized it].

Surrounded by the fourfold assembly, it was as solemn as the first gathering on Vulture Peak; how could there be a distinction between yesterday and this morning? Four flowers fell in profusion as the wondrous Sūtra was first proclaimed;
how could there be any difference between the West and these eastern lands? If you have not yet understood this, I ask that each of you give rise to a heart of joy:
with a single mind contemplate the Buddha, using the Buddha to gather the mind, and using the mind to contemplate the Buddha. When this practice is perfected—
If you understand this point, you should know for yourself that the great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean, and all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes.
In the locus of immeasurable meanings, what further cause for doubt could there be? A question was asked: "What is meant by 'immeasurable meanings'? The Master said:
"The peach is red, the plum is white, and the rose is purple; ginger is pungent, the plum is sour, and the sugarcane is sweet. [The student] said: "If it is thus, then my mind is afraid."
He could not leave. The Master said, "Recognizing one's nature as it flows with the current, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
The monk said, "If that is so, then everywhere the green willows can tether a horse; every household has a road leading to Chang'an. The Master said, "That is still a strain.
The monk asked, "What is the phrase that is without strain? The Master said, "Let the green willows cease tethering the horse. Thereupon, [the monk] attained enlightenment.
"The road is Chang'an. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then the great ocean allows the fish to leap, and the vast sky permits the birds to fly.
The Master said, "That is merely being dissolute. [The monk] asked, "What is the single phrase of the 'Doctrine of the Mean'? The Master said, "One who is ill knows the taste of the meal for himself;
once he has reached home, he does not ask the way."
At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows (extending until: "he caused seven-jeweled stupas to arise").
This section of the sutra reveals the Great Sage’s manifestation of his original essence and his present traces.

The light shines upon eighteen thousand worlds, reaching everywhere without exception; it is thus great, encompassing all that is not, and subtle, entering all that is not excluded. It is clearly and eternally aware, pervading every single atom.
It is not that they are unaware. Within this world, they see those lands in their entirety; thus, there is no interval between the forms and emptiness of the ten directions.
At this Buddha’s location, they hear that Buddha preaching the Dharma; thus, there is no interval in the principle of reality.
Within a single moment, they see all the bhikṣus practicing the myriad deeds, passing through infinite kalpas, attaining Buddhahood, delivering sentient beings, and entering great nirvāṇa.
Later generations erected stupas for them; thus, there has been no interruption throughout the three periods of time and across all ages.

This is because the essence of the wondrous Dharma is none other than the wondrous mind inherently possessed by every person. This wondrous mind is so vast that, beyond the infinite reaches of empty space, one cannot perceive its outer limit.
This wondrous mind is smaller than a minute mote within the infinitesimal dust; yet one cannot see its interior.
This wondrous mind precedes immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet one cannot see its beginning.
This wondrous mind follows endless kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet one cannot see its end. To recognize this wondrous mind is to realize that the four seas are vast.
When the Sages speak of principle, they speak of the principle of this mind.
When the great sages of ten thousand generations practice principle, they practice the principle of this mind.
Because people are ignorant of the principle of this mind, our Buddha, the Great Sage, manifested this wondrous mind in its full perfection within the light between his eyebrows.
The lands of the ten directions are perfectly manifested within this wondrous mind; that is, they are the years and kalpas of the three periods of time.
Because they are the years and kalpas of the three periods of time, one should know that this mind does not go along with what has passed, nor does it come along with what arrives.
If it were to go along with what has passed, then this mind would have already gone along with all that preceded it; how then could there be the awareness of the present? If...
It comes following after what has come; thus, this mind follows after each subsequent thing as it arrives. How could there be an awakening to "today"?
Because this mind is itself the lands of the ten directions, you should know that this mind does not act as a companion to the myriad dharmas.

It does not oppose the various sensory objects (*dhūli*). Because it does not take the myriad phenomena as its companions nor oppose the various sensory objects, one knows that this mind does not become an object by following after things.
If this mind were to become an object by following after things, then seeing mountains would transform them into mountains and seeing water would transform it into water;
how then could there be this present, numinous, and unclouded state, this constant, clear awareness?
He raised his *śalākā* (whisk) and asked, "Do you understand? If you can understand this, you will see that radiant, tranquil illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges.
If this is not yet so, listen again to this verse: This mind fundamentally does not belong to the sense organs or their objects;

Subtle in its entry, vast in its embrace, wondrous and even more divine. It is only because all of you are deluded and do not awaken That the radiance between the eyebrows manifests the primordial body."
Question: What is it that does not belong to the sense organs or their objects? Master: It is utterly devoid of names and designations.
Question: What is the wondrous and divine? Master: One must not allow oneself to be deluded. Question: What is being deluded without awakening?
Master: Mistaking a servant for the master. Question: What is the original body? Master: Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it pervades the ten directions.
Fang said, "If that is so, then everyone is a Buddha; there is no need for further doubt. The Master said, "To open one's mouth is to form a pair of pegs;
to raise an eyebrow is to fall into two or three [categories]."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... [down to] "...beholding and examining the Honored One, what is he about to preach?

This section of the sutra, in broad outline, simply concerns how Maitreya, due to the Buddha’s emission of light which perfectly manifested the ten directions and the three periods of time, gave rise to doubt.
He did not realize that the ten directions and the three periods of time are fundamentally complete within himself; rather, Maitreya himself—
Because [the mind] is narrow, there arise successive layers of questions. For the wondrous nature (miao-xing) of every person is vast and has no exterior;
from the heavens above to the earth below, and all the myriad phenomena in between, none are not the reality of one's own wondrous nature.
Furthermore, the wondrous nature of every person is subtle and has no interior. Since it is subtle and has no interior, throughout the past and present, all that arises in between...
The myriad distinctions are extinguished; there is nothing that is not the substance of my own wondrous nature.
Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions, in every thought-moment, attain equal and perfect enlightenment within this wondrous nature; their bliss becomes ever more blissful.
All sentient beings, in every thought-moment, give rise to views of saṃsāra within this wondrous nature; their suffering becomes ever more suffering. What further doubt can there be?

"How extraordinary! Raising his *nyoi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) staff, he asked: 'Do you understand? If you can understand it here, this is what the World-Honored One realized upon beholding the morning star.
This is what Yuanwu comprehended when he heard the rooster crow.

If you still have further doubts, each of you must sit upon your meditation cushions for thirty years without opening your mouths, and look back again and again at that which existed before your parents were born.'"

Face-to-face for a long time, they are forged into a single whole. One will naturally realize that within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), the provisional names of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" are utterly absent; within the state of equality, there are no images of "self" or "other.
A question was asked: "The principle is fundamentally one; why is it that each does not regard the other? The Master said: "As for 'each not regarding the other,'..."
Because they do not know "one. [The student] asked, "What is this one? The Master said, "The streams, brooks, and ravines all return to the sea;
the hairpins, bracelets, jars, and basins all enter the furnace."
At that time, Mañjuśrī (up to) "therefore manifested this auspicious sign.
This section of the sūtra is Mañjuśrī’s response to Maitreya’s question, stating:

"In the past, within the assemblies of former Buddhas, I have also seen the emission of light perfectly manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions, harmonizing the temporal periods of the three times."
Thereafter, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Today, as the Buddha has now emitted light that perfectly manifests the entire assembly, it is exactly the same as in the past.
I know for certain that the Buddha will surely preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. This section of the sūtra is also called "Citing the Past to Authenticate the Present.
Within the light of the ancient Buddhas, the entirety of the ten directions and the three periods of time was perfectly manifested, preaching the Dharma.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Now, the Buddha fully manifests his entire being throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; he must likewise preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
For this Great Sūtra, within the minds of all Buddhas and great sages, is called "Right Equality" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

it is precisely identical to that which exists throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. It is also called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), as it perfectly encompasses the ten directions and the three periods of time without exception.
There is that which is non-awakened. It is also called the Mahāyāna, for it broadly encompasses the ten directions and the three periods of time, carrying all beings without exception.
It is also called the Middle and the Constant, for it is neither biased nor leaning, neither changing nor altering.
It is also called the Perfect and Perfect Sea of Fruits, for when practitioners reach this state, they have attained the ultimate ground. It is also called the Profound.
This profound and subtle realm cannot be even faintly glimpsed by those of limited wisdom or narrow vision.
Furthermore, it is termed the Dharmakāya, the essence of the Way, the Supreme Ultimate (Tàijí), and the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu).

Even in distant lands and foreign regions, wherever names and titles are established to elucidate the great meaning of this Great Sūtra, they all serve to reveal the primordial mind of the Buddhas and the Great Holy Ones. Indeed.
For a long time, people have not understood this mind. Because they have not understood this mind, our Buddha, the Great Sage, has proclaimed this sutra. To preach this sutra is no ordinary matter;
therefore, our Buddha, the Great Sage, again emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows, within which the worlds of the ten directions appeared perfectly.
The convergence of the temporal cycles of the three periods serves as the omen for the preaching of this Great Sūtra.
If one possesses wisdom, one immediately knows that the World-Honored One has finished preaching the sūtra; he raises his *cintāmaṇi* and asks: "Do you understand? Heh! Ten ages of past and present."
From beginning to end, one does not depart from a single thought. Within the ocean of boundless lands, self and other are not separated by even the tip of a hair.
A question was asked: "What is the raining down of the great Dharma rain? The Master said: "The withered and parched are all renewed at once.

[The questioner] asked: "What is the blowing of the great Dharma conch? The Master said: "The deaf all hear it. [The questioner] asked: "If the withered cannot give rise to seeing, how can the deaf [hear]?"
The student said, "I see this, but I cannot hear it. How is that? The Master said, "The direct and fundamental source is what the Buddha certified. Plucking leaves and seeking branches is not for me.
The student asked, "What is the direct and immediate phrase? The Master said, "Listen to these mountain verses: 'Every person is a Buddha; there is no need for doubt.
Remember these two lines of Zhongfeng’s poem, and you shall become a Buddha this very day.'"
Go! The Master who transforms the Land of Bliss has already considered you too late.
O sons of good family, as in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago...
The single character *kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of this land, it is called "time. *Asaṃkhyeya* is a Sanskrit term;

in the language of this land, it is called "incalculable. That which is incalculable is the greatest number among all numbers—it is inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless—all of which are great numerical figures.
[These terms are used] because the human mind is narrow and views itself as limited.
Failing to awaken to the nature inherently possessed within oneself, this [nature] has no beginning in the past and no end in the future.
Our Buddha, the Great Sage, penetrates the past and present through his radiant light, desiring that every person suddenly awaken to the nature inherently possessed.
Thus it is long; thus it is great. Alas, the delusion of sentient beings is so deep that they still do not...
This is to be understood. This is why Maitreya poses his questions layer upon layer and Mañjuśrī provides his answers layer upon layer.

Although the phrasing is extensive, its general purport is simply to cause every person to suddenly awaken to their inherently possessed nature—which is vast and without exterior, minute and without interior, beginningless in the past and endless in the future. These two lines of the sutra...
Although Mañjuśrī has already cited the most distant [measure], he now intends to reveal the ultimate length. Let us try once more to explain it in detail over an immeasurable period of time.
"Time" here refers to an *kalpa*. Suppose there were a great stone, eight thousand *li* in diameter and thickness;

if one were to wipe it once every hundred years with a light silk cloth weighing only two and a half *qian*, even after this stone had been completely worn away, [the duration would still not have ended]. It is not seen.
A *paramāṇu* (micro-dust) is called a *kalpa*. "Incalculable" refers to an *asaṃkhyeya*, which is the number of *paramāṇus* in a trichiliocosm.
Even a single pinch of dust already contains millions of units; how much more so when the *paramāṇus* of a trichiliocosm are used as the count?
Thus, one thousand worlds constitute what is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍika-lokadhatu*). One thousand [of those]...
One thousand small chiliocosms is called a medium chiliocosm. One thousand medium chiliocosms is what is termed a great trichiliocosm.
Taking all such worlds and reducing them to the number of their constituent atoms is called an *asaṃkhyeya*. An *asaṃkhyeya* is the number of atoms in a great trichiliocosm.
The number of atoms in a great trichiliocosm is called an inconceivable number (*acintya*). Inconceivable...

To deliberate upon the number of atoms in a great trichiliocosm is called the "boundless number" (*ananta-saṃkhyā*). To deliberate upon the number of atoms in boundless great trichiliocosms is called the "immeasurable number" (*apramāṇa-saṃkhyā*).

After a long while, Mañjuśrī cited ancient precedents to illustrate the present: although he wished to manifest that the wondrous nature is inherently possessed by every person, he therefore invoked these vast numbers to expand upon the point.
Nevertheless, this inherently possessed wondrous nature cannot be compared to anything else; it has no equal and nothing can match it.
Although Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom, even by drawing upon collateral citations and indirect metaphors, he cannot exhaust even a ten-thousandth part of this wondrous nature.
Since the wondrous nature is embodied in its entirety, how could it be easily realized? All of you should reflect upon this once more in detail. It was asked:
“The wondrous nature is embodied in form; thus it is difficult to clarify. Tell me, can you clarify it today through this lecture or not?
The Master said, “It would be like placing a single hair in the vast void, or like casting a single drop into a great abyss.
[The student] said, “If that is so, then the Way is boundless and the practitioners are inexhaustible. The Master said, “Who allows you to come and go? [The student] said, “It is just like this...”
"How is it when one sits and cuts off [all attachments]? The Master said: "All Buddhas praise it.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp-Brightness), who taught the Dharma for Bodhisattvas and was protected by the Buddhas' mindfulness.
This section of the sutra is, in broad outline, nothing more than an invocation of the past to corroborate the present; there is no other meaning to it.
Since the beginning of heaven, earth, humans, and things, sages have appeared from time to time, each with different appearances and names.

Yet, if one seeks their inherently good mind, there is no difference among them. Even when establishing words and instituting teachings in diverse regions and distant lands, they likewise [differ in form].
Each is different. Yet when one seeks their words on the goodness of human nature and their teachings on the goodness of human nature, there is no difference between them.

Their heads are capped, their feet shod, their bodies clothed, and their hands held—each of these is different; yet when one seeks their dignified deportment based on the goodness of nature and their reverence based on the goodness of nature, there is no difference between them.
This is because the ways of the world have reached the utmost decadence and the hearts of men are greatly perverse.
Our Buddha, the Great Sage, appeared in the world; he preached the Dharma for over forty years and delivered more than three hundred assemblies of sutras.
Once the minds of people had become pure and the ways of the world were unified in their virtue, he then emitted light to manifest perfectly, revealing his single Dharmakāya.
His intention was to cause every person to suddenly awaken to the single Dharma-body. Yet, alas, the multitude remained deluded;

thus, Maitreya posed his questions layer upon layer. Within these successive inquiries, he integrated past and present into a single thought-moment and condensed the ocean of lands into the tip of a hair.
Alas, those who listened failed to realize this; for this reason, Mañjuśrī also [posed his questions].
In the Master’s layered responses, although he cites the past to corroborate the present, he also fuses the ancient and the modern within a single thought-moment in his verse:

"The ocean of lands is gathered within the tip of a hair. Thus, although immeasurable kalpas ago may be distant, the Buddha’s possession of the ten titles is identical to the present Buddha’s possession of the ten titles;
the excellence of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma then was the same as the excellence of the present Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.

It is the same. Thus, up to the opening of the provisional to reveal the real, the convergence of the three vehicles into the one, and the bestowing of the prediction of entry into *nirvāṇa*, there is no difference whatsoever.
For those who later uphold this teaching, if they are diligent, they will surely achieve success; if they are indolent, they will not fail—there is likewise no difference here.
[The Master] held up his *añjali* and said: "Do you understand? If you can understand it here, the Lamp-Light has never..."
The past—Maitreya, what has the future to do with it? A lump of clay or a clod of earth emits great radiance;
a gourd and a winter melon blaze forth and constantly preach. If this is not yet so, then for now study the wondrous light with diligence;

do not follow the indolence of those who seek fame. He asked: "The general purport of the sutras is simply to gather the branches back into the root. But tell me, how does one pass through the myriad phenomena?"
[The student] said, "Numerous Buddhas have appeared. Why is it that the three realms are still so turbulent? The Master said, "It is simply because you yourself are turbulent within the three realms.
Since antiquity, how has there ever been anything other than the One? [The student] asked, "What can one do about the discrimination occurring before one's eyes?

The Master said, "Even if you discriminate, it is all merely distinguishing the density of flowers in the sky or comparing the length and shortness of a rabbit’s horns. [The student] asked, "What is [this]?"
[The student] said, "There is no discrimination. The Master said, "The peony flower blooms as the face of a Bodhisattva; the palm leaf unfurls as the head of a yakṣa.
[The student] said, "This is still a point of discrimination for a student. The Master said, "That which is capable of discriminating is itself non-discriminative."
At that time, Mañjuśrī... [the Buddha] shall eliminate and sever them until they are exhausted without remainder.
This section of the sūtra is Mañjuśrī’s restatement of what was previously said:

namely, that as it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it is with the present Buddha, and even so it is with the Buddhas of the ten directions; all of them open the three and reveal the one, without duality.
This is the Way. Within the space between Heaven and Earth, only man is most spiritual. The sovereign of a person’s body is nothing other than the single character "nature" (xing).
If nature is clear, then morality, righteousness, benevolence, propriety, ritual, and transformation will all be clear;
there will be nothing that is not so. Now, as for this nature: within the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth, it is called "principle" (li). Therefore it is said: "Within the universe..."

In essence, there is but a single principle. Within me, this principle, when particularized as the nature-and-principle, is called emotion (*qing*). Therefore it is said: "The three realms cannot be transcended; only emotion constitutes an obstruction.
If one can truly overcome and eliminate the emotions within oneself, there will be nothing but a single mass of celestial nature.

Then, every thought-moment will be the lamp-light of preaching the Dharma, and every phenomenon will be the wondrous radiance of expounding the sutras. Thus, the six perfections and myriad practices [are spontaneously fulfilled].
It is primordially and spontaneously perfected; the four virtues and three bodies are ultimately not obtained from another. Should this not yet be the case, you must examine it closely in stillness:

from the time this body was first born, whether for ten years, twenty years, or even seventy or eighty years—though these years are seen to have passed—one has never been transmigrated by the passing of those years.
But what, then, is this thing? One immediately knows that since this mind does not follow what has already passed, it certainly does not follow what comes later.
Since it does not follow what comes later, it likewise does not abide in the present. Thus one knows that this mind has no initial phrase, no final phrase, and no present phrase.
Because there is no past, future, or present, the three periods of time cannot [grasp it].
Because it undergoes transformation and change, even the empty space of the ten directions cannot encompass it.

Since empty space cannot encompass it, one knows that this mind extends vertically through the three periods of time and pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions. Holding up his *añjali* (hands joined), he said: "Do you understand?"
I have seen such a premonitory sign of light from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; by this, I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
If it were otherwise, the Buddha would surely sever the doubts and regrets of those seeking the three vehicles, so that none remain at all.
[The interlocutor] asks: "The Dharma Master Miaoguang was a previous incarnation of Mañjuśrī. Maitreya—"
“The Bodhisattva is the subsequent substance of seeking names. “If that is so, then the present and the ancient are distinct and clear.

Why, then, do you also say that fundamentally there is neither present nor ancient? The Master said, “The present is simply the present; the ancient is simply the ancient. One who knows the present and the ancient finds that, fundamentally, there is no present and no ancient.
[The student] said, “If this is so, then by following the flow one recognizes one’s nature; there is neither joy nor sorrow. The Master said, “If you maintain [this view]...”
Recognizing each character: "From three thousand *li* away, one asks for Chang'an. [The student] asked, "How is it so? The Master said, "I do not permit you to speak of it.
[The student] said, "In that case, opening the mouth forms a pair of pegs; raising the eyebrows falls into two or three. The Master said, "Listen to this mountain verse:
Within this, there is fundamentally no past or present; manifesting in various forms, he is named Avalokiteśvara. All people..."
If you wish to behold the face of Avalokiteśvara, the mountain is naturally high and the water is naturally deep.
Chapter Two: "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*).

"Expedient means" (*upāya*) carries the sense of adapting to circumstances and employing skillful methods. It is like a great city that, according to where people come from, [provides them with appropriate access]. It is not...
It is like a single path: if those coming from the east enter through the eastern gate, and those coming from the west enter through the western gate, it is convenient;

otherwise, it is not. For although the complete and perfect wondrous nature is inherently possessed by every person, even if a Buddha or a sage possessed great eloquence, they could never point it out in its entirety.

...it is indeed so. One must take the sprouts that have already emerged and, by drawing out various analogies and singing them from different angles, cause the person to awaken to this for themselves;

"In its own nature (*svabhāva*), there is fundamentally no principle of desiring to kill. This is how one teaches them not to kill living beings. Or, if someone steals what another holds dear, one immediately points out: "In its own nature..."

In this manner, even when people limit themselves by their own views and experiences, one points to them and says: "The self-nature is vast and expansive, encompassing all of space.
When people shorten themselves by means of birth and death, one points to them and says: "The self-nature is eternally enduring; its beginning and end cannot be fathomed."

"Watch the spirit in the soaring hawk and leaping fish; otherwise, if you wish to exercise expedient means, you will willingly become an outsider to the gate of busyness.

Finally, we shall examine them by fusing them with the term "Chan. *Samādhi* is a Sanskrit word from the Western lands. In the language of this country (China), it is called "Right Reception" (*zhèngshòu*). "Right" (*zhèng*)...
Concentration rectifies the mind. To have a rectified mind means to be free from the habitual tendencies within the mind.

it is the ultimate of sincerity. When sincerity reaches its ultimate, one is able to plan the great patterns, establish the Great Dharma, and transform and nourish all things.

When one reaches the pinnacle of sagehood, the people revere him upon seeing him, believe him upon hearing his words, and rejoice in his conduct.

Since right reception is the ultimate state of sagehood and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the height of sincerity, it is the constant state of having reached the center of the mind; thus, he is a Great Sage.
The mind is like a cloudless sky or still water, like the brilliant sun or refined gold, without the slightest flaw.

The capacity of the Great Sage is like empty space, encompassing all existence; it is like parents nurturing their children;
it possesses its own abundance. How great is the nature of the Sage! It takes the ten directions and the three periods of time as one.
As for its substance, it takes the six realms and four modes of birth as a single body.
Such perfect fusion and wondrous harmony cannot be fully extolled, cannot be exhausted by exposition, cannot be reached through practice, and cannot be matched by analogy;
it is given the provisional name "samādhi. How easy is it to realize and enter this samādhi? Within this samādhi, our Buddha does not perceive...

Yet, there are indeed such things as the middle, the internal, the external, the front, and the back; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Buddha.
Question: The exposition has been clear. Now tell me, what is Chan? The Master said: "Like being struck by a staff."

The Master said, "Śāriputra, you should know that the wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable (up to: that which cannot be known."
This section of the sutra states that the mind of the Great Sage of the world cannot be known by anyone; it cannot be recognized by anyone.

For the mind of the Most Holy Buddhas has no time—neither past, future, nor present—and no direction—neither east, west, south, north, above, nor below—and no name of a sentient being by which it can be named.
There are no realms of heaven or hell that can be taken as objective domains. It is all-pervasive, lofty, and brilliant; vast, expansive, and pure.
Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it pervades the ten directions. Because it pervades the ten directions horizontally, this mind has no interval between space and form.
Because it exhausts the three periods vertically, this mind has no interval between past and present. Since there is no interval between past and present...

When the intervals between the past and future limits are severed, and the space between form and emptiness is transcended, then internal and external sentiments are forgotten, and one returns to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
When the past and future limits are severed, one is the original, single Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Precisely in such a state, there is no ceiling above and no bottom below; there are no boundaries on the sides and no place of abiding in the center. This is the fundamental teaching.
It is called the Perfect Body (*yuan-ti*); it is the Pure Dharma-body (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*). In Confucianism, it is called the Original Way (*yuandao*);
it is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) arising from the Poleless Ultimate (*wuji*). In the Laozi teaching, it is called the One; it is the Great Dao of the Poleless Ultimate.
Yet this mind can be known through observation and inquiry. Those who know it through observation and inquiry are the wise of the world. There are those who awaken to this mind.
Thus they practice, gradually transforming their former minor tendencies; such are the sages and philosophers of the world.
Those whose cultivation is pure and unified, yet still retain traces of discriminative thought, are the lesser sages of the world.
Indeed, the minds of all sages are perfect and vast, equaling the encompassing and supporting of heaven and earth, and equaling the illumination of the sun and moon.
"Facing [the world]. He embodies the nature and emotions of the myriad things to establish his teaching; therefore, all that possesses blood and breath revere and love him.

"Willingly removing all barriers, one remains as before a person of great family. A questioner asked, "What is the wisdom of the Buddhas?

Therefore, it is not yet difficult to carry dry grass into a blazing great fire without it being burned; what is truly difficult is to read this sūtra even for a moment.

Thus, it extends even to their principles and affairs; only the Buddha is profoundly deep, such that no one in the world can equal him.

From "the true reality of all dharmas" up to "ultimately equal"—this section of the sutra speaks of the true reality of all dharmas as the myriad phenomena before one's eyes; this is precisely the intended meaning of the sublime and wondrous original text of the sutra.
The ultimate reality perfectly realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions is precisely the intrinsically present enlightened nature of sentient beings.
The intrinsically present enlightened nature of sentient beings is precisely the states of worldly transmigration—of suffering and joy, rising and falling.
This is because sentient beings do not awaken to all phenomena, do not understand all phenomena, and do not know them.
All phenomena (dharmas) are utterly deluded and obscure. Upon these objects, one gives rise to evil thoughts and commits evil deeds;
dying here and being born there, one wanders through the cycle of existence, suffering endlessly.

Therefore, the Great Sage pointed to these phenomena and called them dreams and illusions, bubbles and shadows, so that people might seek within the realm of these phenomena that which is signless and nameless.
The truth that is immovable and unchanging. Those of the Śrāvaka Hīnayāna do not recognize the perfect principle of all phenomena;
regarding this realm, they loathe suffering and seek pleasure, and by destroying their attachment to existence, they cling to emptiness.

Therefore, the Great Sage further points out that these very phenomena are themselves true emptiness and themselves wondrous existence, so that people may seek [enlightenment] within this realm of all phenomena.
This is the enlightened nature of perfect interfusion and wondrous assembly.

Because Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna do not yet know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they undergo arduous cultivation through kalpa after kalpa and exert their strength life after life, striving to deliver all sentient beings and necessarily realizing the ultimate Great Way.
Therefore, the Great Sage further points out that all phenomena are themselves the true reality, which is itself the *dharmatā*. That is to say...
This is the principle of the Buddha; it is the wondrous reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. To engage with this, the Confucians call it "investigating things" (*gewu*);

to awaken to this, they call it "extending knowledge" (*zhizhi*). When knowledge reaches its limit and things are investigated, then the reality-mark of all phenomena is clearly and constantly known, manifest and never obscured.
Thus, from the cultivation of the self, the regulation of the family, the governance of the state, to the bringing of peace to the world—there is nothing that does not become efficacious.

This is verified by the fact that from transcending birth and death throughout all past and present, to the sudden entry into *nirvāṇa* from top to bottom, there is nothing that does not respond with wondrous efficacy.
Holding up his *añjali* (wish-fulfilling jewel), he said: "Do you understand?

If you can understand it here, then the straightness of the pine and the curvature of the thorn, the whiteness of the crane and the blackness of the crow—all are the substance of the *dharmatā*. As for delusion regarding life and awakening regarding the Buddha, these are matters of..."
Worldly principles and ultimate truth are both the functioning of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Should this not be so, tomorrow I shall once again untangle this web of complications for you all.
He asked: "If all phenomena before one's eyes are the true mark, why do people fail to awaken to them?"
The Master said, "It is not that you do not awaken; it is simply that you are unwilling to awaken. The student said, "I have been practicing for many years, Master.
It is not that I am unwilling to awaken. The Master said, "If you are willing to awaken, what is there left to ask today? The student asked, "What is it like when one is willing to awaken?

From "The true reality of all dharmas" to "the ultimate equality of beginning and end" (repeated).
Regarding this section of the sutra, the various masters of Nanyue and Tiantai each offered different expositions; however, the exposition by Master Huan of Wenzhou is the most pertinent.
Now, let us examine it once more according to Master Huan’s interpretation. As for "true reality" (*bhūtatathatā*), it is precisely the marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Yet this reality is of the same essence as the Great Sages of the ten directions throughout antiquity, without distinction;

it is perfectly constant, luminous, and wondrous, a dharma-nature that undergoes no further change or differentiation. Nevertheless, this dharma-nature can be fully exhausted and realized only by Buddha after Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.

Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively realize the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). As for "all phenomena," the myriad things of heaven and earth, though diverse and manifold, do not transcend ten categories of phenomena.
These ten categories are: first, mark (*lakṣaṇa*); second, nature (*svabhāva*); third, essence (*bhāva*); fourth, power (*bala*); fifth, activity (*kriyā*); sixth, cause (*hetu*); seventh...
8. Conditions; 9. Fruits; 10. The ultimate consummation of the beginning and the end. Regarding "the ultimate consummation of the beginning and the end":
all myriad phenomena before one's eyes each possess a fundamental origin and a final destination; each possesses an ultimate limit and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
For example, the table, incense burner, pine trees, peach trees, people, and other such things before one cannot be fully exhausted [in their origins].
To exhaustively reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) yet not call it "investigating things" (*gewu*);

to be unable to thoroughly investigate the root yet not call it "contemplating Zen" (*chanchan*), nor call it "thorough awakening" (*che-wu*), nor call it "attaining knowledge" (*zhizhi*)—only when one attains knowledge and achieves thorough awakening [can these names be truly applied].

Then, regarding the table before you, the incense burner, the pine tree, and the human figure—there is nothing that cannot be resolved and nothing that cannot be examined from its beginning to its end.
Furthermore, examine this by carefully analyzing it through the ten dharmas once more. As for "retribution" (*pāpa*), it refers to the fruit as the result;
just as when a peach tree bears fruit, the ripening of that fruit constitutes the retribution. As for "fruit" (*phala*), it refers to the conditions.
"Ripening" refers to the fruit. It is like a peach tree that has already blossomed and formed fruit;

when it reaches the season of fragrant ripeness through the nourishment of rain and dew and the cultivation of manure and soil, this is what is meant. "Conditions" (pratyaya) means assisting the cause as a condition.
For instance, although a peach tree may have blossomed and flourished, if it lacks the assistance of rain, dew, and the cultivation of manure and soil, it will ultimately not [ripen].
Regarding "that which can bring about its own flourishing, its own blossoming, and its own fruition": the "cause" (*hetu*) refers to that which provides the initial basis;
for example, although a peach tree may flourish before one's eyes, its root must necessarily have had a first day of origin. The "agent" (*kartṛ*) refers to that which initiates the action;
for example, although a peach tree has a first day of origin, the intention to plant the peach was what suddenly gave rise to it.
It is not the inherent nature (*prakṛti*). "Power" (*li*) refers to the utility as power; it is like a peach tree when it reaches the time of fragrance and ripeness:
one obtains its flavor by eating it, and one obtains its wealth by selling it. "Substance" (*ti*) refers to the formation of form as substance;
it is like a peach tree where the flowers or fruits, branches and leaves, are distinct and diverse, yet the root is deep and substantial. "Nature" (*xing*) refers to...

Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are fundamentally the nature (svabhāva). For example, just as a single peach tree is a characteristic, there must necessarily also be the root-nature of that single peach tree.
As for characteristics, they are visible as characteristics; for example, when a single peach tree blooms and bears fruit, everyone sees it.
Regarding its nature and its reality, its beginning and its ultimate end—no one knows them.
Therefore, only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively understand them with complete clarity and without falsehood. Although other sages possess illumination, they cannot fathom them to the utmost.
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena" (up to "the ultimate beginning and end").
This section of the sutra has already been expounded twice; now it is for the third time. Listeners, do not grow weary of this repetition.
