Beyond these ten dharmas, one may exhaustively transcend the aggregates without remainder.

This "one such characteristic" refers collectively to the myriad phenomena of phenomenal existence—their manifold diversities and transformations—which are the very forms and appearances visible to the eye. Yet, as for this characteristic:

Those of lesser sages, who lack the inconceivable great eye that vertically exhausts the three periods of time and horizontally pervades the ten directions, are restricted by the narrowness of worldly hearing and seeing;
thus, although their marks may be visible, they cannot be fully exhausted without remainder.
Therefore, only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this. Second, as for "suchness" (*tathatā*):

although my own form and that of the myriad things differ, when one investigates their fundamental source, there is nothing that is not one. This oneness is precisely *xing* (nature); *xing* is precisely *li* (principle).
Although this nature and this principle have two names, they possess no dual substance. Thus, we provisionally designate it as "nature," and nature...

That which is vast yet has no exterior, minute yet has no interior; without beginning in front and without end behind—this the great sages and wise men point to as Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue), the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji), the Great Way (Dadao), the Primordial Substance (Yuanti), the Sovereign God (Shangdi), the Luminous Virtue (Mingde), and the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong).
The Dharma-body likewise cannot exhaustively manifest this nature, which is vast and profound, a deep spring, and fully endowed with all greatness.
Therefore it is said: "Only Buddha and Buddha can thoroughly exhaust [it]," extending even to such a body and such power.
"It is thus made; it is thus caused; it is thus conditioned; its beginning, end, and ultimate reality are all equal. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this;
it is not something that minor sages of the world can fully know. Raising his *niyue* (wish-fulfilling jewel) staff, he said:
"Do you understand? If you can understand this, you may say: 'The Way is the abiding of dharmas in their respective positions; it is the phenomenal aspect of the world.'"
It is eternally abiding. If it were otherwise, you must go into a quiet room, burn incense, and sit in silence, investigating this *nyoi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) in the hands of this mountain monk:
what was it before ten million kalpas? And what will it be after ten million kalpas?
When your practice becomes pure and mature and is forged into a single whole, you will spontaneously realize the nature of past and present.
Without departing from the present moment, the ocean of lands is not separated from the tip of a single hair. To speak of this is truly only for Buddha after Buddha. He asked:
"What is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena? The Master said: "Only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom it. He asked again: "How so?"
"If it is so, then the multitude does not understand. The Master said, "It is not that they do not understand; they simply refuse to believe.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like when they do believe? The Master said, "The entire earth is pure gold."
"Such is its substance, such is its power" (up to) "the beginning and the end are ultimately equal" (is repeated).
Form is the substance; utility is the power. That is to say, where there is such a substantial characteristic, there is such utility.
For example, if one possesses the physical form of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, then one has the power to transform the three thousandfold world system.
As for its utility: if there is a substance that is pure and pervasive of all places, then there is the utility of pervading the ten directions and penetrating the three periods of time.
If there is the form of an ox, then there is the utility of plowing and tilling.
When the form of a horse is complete, it possesses the utility of galloping and driving;

likewise, even such things as the "cutting of grass" and the "carving of man," the "carving of amaranth and *rājika*," the transformation of mercury into gold, the solidification of quicksilver by sulfur, and the great medicinal herb of the lotus [are possible].
To wear it is to attain a lifespan equal to the sun and moon; to recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī is to become a peer of heaven and earth—these are all sayings we hear constantly.

Yet, as for the great principle and great power where "to direct the mind is already an error" and "to stir a thought is already to deviate," even the mouth of Kātyāyanīputra could not discourse upon them, nor could the wisdom of Śāriputra fathom them. Furthermore...
Who could possibly perceive its complete form and understand its utility?
Since one cannot fully know its form, its utility, its function, its causes, and even its beginning and end in their ultimate equality, [how could one know it all?]
Furthermore, how could anyone else know it exhaustively? Therefore it is said: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can investigate and exhaust [this matter];
others, lacking such penetration, do not know it, and cannot know it exhaustively. Holding up his *añjali* (jewel-in-hand) gesture, he asks: "Do you understand?

If you can understand this, you will realize past and present in a single thought-moment and encompass the ocean of lands within the tip of a hair. Should this not be so, then for now, turn toward stillness."
Silently observe once more: from where does life come? To where does death go? Suddenly, one attains realization:
one must know for oneself that the golden bird at the bottom of the sea is the sun in the heavens; the infant within the eye is the person before one’s face.
What more need be said of "only a Buddha with a Buddha can exhaustively fathom this"? Aha! Listen further to this verse: "Heaven and earth differ in ten thousand ways and a thousand distinctions."

Essence: The fundamental source is but one body; within this single body and mind, all things are also one. Every head and every object is entirely the True Nature. Question: What is the cause for attaining Buddhahood? Master: Practice goodness with diligence. Question: [How does one do so? Master: [Practice. Question: [What is that practice? Master: [To act in accordance with the Way. Question: [How does one know if it is correct? Master: [By observing whether one’s actions accord with the Dharma. Question: [If one acts contrary to the Dharma, what happens? Master: [One will surely fall into the three evil realms. Question: [If one acts in accordance with the Dharma, what happens? Master: [One will surely attain Buddhahood. Question: [How can one know for certain? Master: [By examining one’s own mind. Question: [How does one examine one’s own mind? Master: [By seeing whether one’s thoughts are pure or defiled. Question: [If one’s thoughts are pure, what is the result? Master: [One will surely attain Buddhahood. Question: [If one’s thoughts are defiled, what is the result? Master: [One will surely fall into the three evil realms. Question: [How can one ensure one’s thoughts remain pure? Master: [By constantly practicing mindfulness. Question: [How does one practice mindfulness? Master: [By not allowing the mind to wander toward external objects. Question: [If the mind wanders toward external objects, what happens? Master: [One will surely lose the Way. Question: [If the mind does not wander toward external objects, what happens? Master: [One will surely attain the Way. Question: [How can one ensure the mind does not wander toward external objects? Master: [By cultivating the power of concentration. Question: [How does one cultivate the power of concentration? Master: [By sitting in meditation. Question: [How does one sit in meditation? Master: [By letting the mind rest in its natural state. Question: [What is the natural state of the mind? Master: [It is originally empty and still. Question: [If the mind is originally empty and still, why do we experience suffering and joy? Master: [Because of deluded thoughts. Question: [How can we eliminate deluded thoughts? Master: [By realizing that they have no inherent substance. Question: [If deluded thoughts have no inherent substance, how can they arise? Master: [They arise from the false clinging of the ignorant mind. Question: [How can we sever this false clinging? Master: [By awakening to the True Mind. Question: [What is the True Mind? Master: [It is the nature of the Buddha. Question: [How can we realize the nature of the Buddha? Master: [By practicing the Six Paramitas. Question: [How does one practice the Six Paramitas? Master: [By giving away wealth, observing the precepts, practicing patience, exerting vigor, practicing dhyana, and cultivating wisdom. Question: [What is the ultimate goal of these practices? Master: [To return to the Source and realize the Great Enlightenment. Question: [How does one realize the Great Enlightenment? Master: [By attaining the Unconditioned Wisdom. Question: [What is Unconditioned Wisdom? Master: [It is the wisdom that is free from all conceptualization. Question: [How does one attain this wisdom? Master: [By cutting off all attachments. Question: [What is meant by "cutting off all attachments? ] Master: [It means to let go of the self and the dharmas. Question: [How does one let go of the self and the dharmas? Master: [By realizing that both are empty. Question: [What is the realization of emptiness? Master: [It is the cessation of all false thinking. Question: [How does one cease all false thinking? Master: [By maintaining the state of non-arising. Question: [What is the state of non-arising? Master: [It is the original face of the Buddha. Question: [How does one see the original face of the Buddha? Master: [By looking inward with a clear and focused mind. Question: [What is the result of seeing the original face of the Buddha? Master: [One will become a Buddha. Question: [How does one become a Buddha? Master: [By manifesting the Ten Powers and the Four Fearlessnesses. Question: [What are the Ten Powers and the Four Fearlessnesses? Master: [They are the qualities of a Tathagata. Question: [How does one attain the qualities of a Tathagata? Master: [By fulfilling the Bodhisattva path. Question: [How does one fulfill the Bodhisattva path? Master: [By practicing the Ten Stages. Question: [What are the Ten Stages? Master: [They are the stages of Dry Wisdom, the Stage of Heat, the Stage of Patience, the Stage of the World’s First Dharma, the Stage of Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiance, the Stage of Difficult Victory, the Stage of Presence, and the Stage of Far-Reaching. Question: [What is the final stage? Master: [The Stage of Cloud of Dharma. Question: [What is the Cloud of Dharma? Master: [It is the stage where one’s wisdom is like a vast cloud covering the entire universe. Question: [How does one reach this stage? Master: [By perfecting all virtues. Question: [What is the perfection of all virtues? Master: [It is the completion of the Six Paramitas. Question: [What is the completion of the Six Paramitas? Master: [It is the total dedication of all roots of goodness toward the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Question: [What is Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Master: [It is the supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas. Question: [How does one attain supreme, perfect enlightenment? Master: [By realizing the identity of samsara and nirvana. Question: [What is the identity of samsara and nirvana? Master: [It is the absence of duality. Question: [What is the absence of duality? Master: [It is the realization that there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be abandoned. Question: [How does one realize this? Master: [By entering the gate of Non-dual Dharma. Question: [What is the gate of Non-dual Dharma? Master: [It is the gate of the Middle Way. Question: [What is the Middle Way? Master: [It is the way that transcends all extremes. Question: [How does one transcend all extremes? Master: [By dwelling in the state of equanimity. Question: [What is the state of equanimity? Master: [It is the state where there is neither subject nor object. Question: [How does one dwell in the state where there is neither subject nor object? Master: [By being free from all conceptualization. Question: [What is freedom from all conceptualization? Master: [It is the state of Great Nirvana. Question: [What is Great Nirvana? Master: [It is the ultimate liberation of all beings. Question: [How does one achieve ultimate liberation? Master: [By realizing the true nature of reality. Question: [What is the true nature of reality? Master: [It is the Dharmakaya. Question: [How does one realize the Dharmakaya? Master: [By attaining the Great Mirror Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks. Question: [What are the Four Wisdoms? Master: [They are the four modes of enlightened cognition. Question: [How does one attain the four modes of enlightened cognition? Master: [By perfecting the Ten Paramitas. Question: [What is the teaching of the Dharma according to their capacities? Master: [It is the manifestation of various skillful means. Question: [What are the various skillful means? Master: [They include the Three Vehicles, the Five Vehicles, and the One Vehicle. Question: [What is the One Vehicle? Master: [It is the Mahayana. Question: [What is the Mahayana? Master: [It is the vehicle that carries all beings to the other shore. Question: [How does one carry all beings to the other shore? Master: [By bestowing the gift of the Dharma. Thus is the action, thus is the cause, thus is the condition, thus is the fruit, and thus is the retribution. (He spoke again.)
The initial arising is called "action" (*karma*); that which provides the beginning is called the "cause" (*hetu*); that which assists the cause is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*);

the ripening of conditions is called the "fruit" (*phala*); and the response to the fruit is called the "retribution" (*vipāka*). For example, if a person suddenly gives rise to a single thought of harming another, taking this mind as the beginning, and later encounters others with the same desire to harm that person who assist them, then the initial thought of harming the person is established.
It is accomplished. Once a deed that harms others has been completed, how could there not be a subsequent retribution that harms oneself?
Furthermore, suppose a person suddenly gives rise to a single thought of the desire to become a Buddha. Taking this mind as the beginning, they do not cease from moment to moment.
Later, meeting another who likewise desires to become a Buddha as a condition, they practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds together. Thus, the thirty-two [marks]...
The marks and the eighty minor characteristics—the Buddha-fruit adorned with myriad virtues—will certainly be realized.
Once the Buddha-fruit is realized, humans and devas will look up in reverence and the ten directions will offer praise; how could this not be the retribution for the fruit of the response?
All the myriad dharmas of the world do not, in total, transcend these ten dharmas of nature, marks, and so forth. Furthermore, these ten dharmas do not, in turn, transcend nature and marks.
Regarding the four characters "cause and effect" (*hetu-phala*): because there is such a cause, there must be such an effect;
because there is such a characteristic, one must possess such a nature. As the ancient sages said: "When Heaven produces the masses of the people, there are things and there are their norms.
It is also said: "What you send forth shall return to you. This is what the world calls "planting melons and harvesting melons; planting beans and harvesting beans."
"Performing good, one encounters good; performing evil, one encounters evil. Furthermore, karma is created because of the mind; it follows from the awakening of one's nature.
When conditions ripen, they become fruit; the fruit is the manifestation of the nature. Thus, nature, manifestation, cause, and effect revolve through successive ascent and descent.

This section of the sūtra, in brief, reiterates the two kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas: the provisional and the ultimate.
As for provisional wisdom, it employs phenomena to clarify principles; it utilizes worldly letters, words, and language to clarify the ultimate reality that is devoid of letters, words, and language.
As for true wisdom, it is the substantial reality of all phenomena; it cannot be manifested by letters, nor can it be concealed by speech.
It is without arising and without cessation, without formation and without destruction. It is not like the temporary, borrowed, and unreal path.
The Buddhas of the ten directions—the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, and the Buddhas of the future—establish [this teaching] through their instruction.
The Dharma-banner [Bodhisattva] delivers sentient beings; there are none who are not transformed and saved by means of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
Yet, while the provisional wisdom provisionally establishes the Three Vehicles and the real wisdom truly reveals the One Dharma, people all fail to understand the original intent of the Buddhas.
This original intent of the Buddhas does not merely consist in praising their own two wisdoms of the provisional and the real; it solely desires to reveal [the truth] to others.
Human beings fundamentally possess the essence of perfect and eternal awakening. It is so vast that nothing is greater than it; so minute that nothing is smaller than it.
It has no beginning, yet nothing precedes it; it has no end, yet nothing follows it.

Indeed, because sentient beings are deluded regarding this essence of perfect and eternal awakening, they wander through the six realms of existence; whereas the Buddhas, having awakened to it, transcend all phenomena. Furthermore, this...
The essence of perfect, eternal awakening is the fundamental root of all sentient beings and Buddhas, the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the *dharmadhātu* and *tathatā*.
Therefore, while the Buddhas awaken to it and remain eternally one, sentient beings are deluded and remain eternally manifold.

Because they are eternally manifold, all sentient beings are ultimately unable to reunite within the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). Because it is eternally one, the Buddhas of the ten directions [remain eternally one].
It cannot be dispersed or flowed away within the realm of sentient beings. Holding up his *niwan* (wish-fulfilling jewel) and saying, "Do you understand?

There are those who realize the fruit of a śrāvaka, those who realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and those who realize the fruit of a bodhisattva; all are skillfully enticed and led [to liberation].
"Liberation" means being free from suffering and detached from attachment. Generally, there are many kinds of suffering, but they are all comprised within three.

Likewise, there are many kinds of attachment, which are also comprised within three. These three attachments are: first, attachment to the self; second, attachment to objects; and third, attachment to emotions. Regarding attachment to emotions:

because one is deluded by forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and so forth, one clings to them with lingering emotion and refuses to let go; therefore, it is called "attachment. Attachment gives rise to suffering.

Regarding "attachment to objects": because one does not realize that form, sound, fragrance, taste, and so forth are, in their very essence, the Truth itself, one engages in various conceptual discriminations regarding these objects—grasping and rejecting, loving and hating—and thus it is called "attachment. Attachment gives rise to suffering. Regarding "attachment to self":
Because one does not awaken to the fact that the originally inherent Dharmakāya is vast and without exterior, subtle and without interior, beginningless in the past, and endless in the future,
one mistakes this physical body born of parents for the self. Because one mistakes this body for the self,
there arise the greed and aversion of birth and death, and the longing and loathing of ascending and descending.
Because there is greed, evil, and the relishing of joy or aversion, immeasurable suffering follows accordingly. There are three types of suffering: first, the suffering of death;
second, the suffering of blades and staves; and third, the suffering of not obtaining what one desires. As for the suffering of not obtaining what one desires:

it is because one does not realize that forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and so forth are entirely like dreams and illusions, yet one clings to them in various ways; thus, though one seeks them, they cannot be obtained.
This is called suffering. Regarding the suffering of blades and sticks: because one covets forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and so forth, and when such craving is not fulfilled, anger arises;
consequently, others inflict blades and sticks. Since the action was committed by oneself, the retribution is likewise inevitable.

Thus, one undergoes hundreds of kinds of oppression from the blades and sticks of others, and for this reason it is called suffering. Regarding the suffering of death: because one possesses the physical form born of parents.
Death is inevitable. Once dead, one is forever parted from the world; this body cannot be revived thereafter. Therefore, it is called suffering.

Thus, these three types of suffering and three attachments are all due to failing to awaken to the inherently pure *dharmakāya* and instead becoming attached to various sensory objects, resulting in hundreds of forms of painful experience.
For this reason, the Buddhas and great sages employ various skillful means to teach and transform [beings].
To be free from attachment is to be liberated from suffering. [The Master] held up his *ruci* (wish-fulfilling gem) and said: "Do you understand?

Worldly people are deluded regarding this wondrous nature; they follow the transformations of external objects, which is why there are the six realms and four modes of birth.

To cast all myriad phenomena together as a single gold; to melt all ten thousand ages into a single thought.

Zhao said: "This body is merely the physical form bequeathed by one's parents. Which of these is the self-nature that existed before one's parents were born?

Thus, as you investigate and investigate in this manner, regardless of how much effort you expend, there will surely come a time of great awakening. When that moment arrives...
At the time of great awakening, one must certainly have self-confidence that the forms seen by the eyes are the entire body of the wondrous Dharma;
the sounds heard by the ears are the perfect proclamation of the wondrous Dharma; the fragrances and stenches smelled by the nose are the ultimate faith of the wondrous Dharma;

The mind is the condition. The soaring of hawks and leaping of fish, the movement of clouds and the falling of rain—there is nothing that is not the complete essence and great function of the wondrous Dharma.

Because every person is fully endowed with this nature, being thus fully endowed with this nature, they are fully endowed with this [Dharma].
This principle is already fully complete. If this principle is complete, then this mind, these dharmas, and this Way are all complete and perfect without exception.
It is simply that people are unwilling to investigate within stillness for themselves or to exhaustively examine the truth for themselves.

Each and every person has been deluded for a long time; none have awakened on their own. Our Buddha, the Great Sage, has therefore appeared in the world, desiring that every person awaken to the wondrous nature inherently possessed within them.
His desire for all people to awaken to this nature is what is called the "One Great Matter of Cause and Condition.
This is termed the One Great Matter of Cause and Condition because, among the myriad affairs and myriad things of the world, it is the greatest.
As for heaven and earth, down to the finest motes of dust, since they possess form, they will ultimately undergo decay and destruction.

Since they are subject to decay and destruction, they are not my wondrous nature (*miao-xing*) or true reality (*shi-xiang*). Since they are neither wondrous nature nor true reality, they are but deluded thoughts within that nature.

Since they are deluded thoughts within the nature, they are also not the substantial entity of the wondrous principle (*miao-li*). Since they are not the substantial entity of the wondrous principle...
How could its essence be anything other than the wondrous mind and the wondrous Way? By means of this wondrous nature, it pervades all things without distinction;
it manifests through the myriad phenomena as the ultimate spirit. It is able to act as the sovereign of all forms, yet it is not a thing that withers along with the four seasons.
By means of these myriad existences—vast as heaven and earth, minute as a speck of dust—they arise and cease, coming and going in succession.
Therefore, it is called a "small matter. Yet by means of this wondrous nature, it is vast without exterior and subtle without interior;
it neither arises nor ceases, and it neither goes nor comes. Therefore, it is called a "great matter.

The deeds practiced by a bodhisattva do not cling to any signs, nor do they depart from any signs;
every thought-moment is purely true, and their conduct is perfectly equal. Because their conduct is perfectly equal, they will certainly attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect equality.
Moment by moment, one is purely true. One will certainly reach the Buddha’s perfect and complete purity.

All of them employ skillful means to elucidate the individual "nature" (*xing*) character. Nature is precisely the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). [My] faculties are crude and my learning shallow; my realization is likewise—
There is a school of thought. Let us try once more to examine the Buddha-nature by taking it up again. Now, as for this "nature," it is the principle of each and every individual's own mind.
This principle is supremely impartial, supremely level, supremely luminous, supremely great, supremely singular, and supremely perfect.

Therefore, that which appears to be non-partial, non-level, non-luminous, non-great, non-singular, or non-perfect is not because the nature itself is imperfect or non-singular. It is simply that [the deluded mind] fails to realize it.
It is not that they are insufficiently great, insufficiently luminous, insufficiently impartial, or insufficiently balanced; rather, each acts according to their own self-interest and partiality.
Because of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), they are bound by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and constrained by the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

Consequently, they are unable to reach a state of perfect impartiality free from bias and selfishness, a state of perfect balance free from high and low, a state of perfect clarity free from obscurity, a state of perfect vastness free from narrowness, and a state of ultimate oneness.
It is without confusion and, reaching perfection, is without deficiency.
When our Buddha, the Great Sage, appeared, he was simultaneously awakened first and proclaimed the teachings alongside the Great Sages who appeared in various lands throughout the ten directions.

It is endowed with its own nature; like space merging with space, the great trichiliocosm is entirely of golden hue, and even the lands of a single mote of dust are universally of white jade.
Pervading from the highest to the lowest, the radiance is brilliantly clear; it is both principle and phenomenon, perfectly equal and perfectly round.
When one has reached this stage, what can be said of "resolved" or "unresolved," or "awakened" or "unawakened"?

[The monk] said, "The words of the Master are sincere; how could I dare not believe them? The Master said, "Since you can believe with such clarity, it is certainly you. [The monk] asked, "What then?

This means that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he observed that the capacities of sentient beings were narrow and limited, and that they lacked merit and wisdom; he therefore gradually guided and enticed them toward the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Although the six classes of beings differ in their rising and sinking, they all enter the perilous path of birth and death.

They are indeed the same. Why, then, is it called a perilous path? It is because every person inherently possesses the wondrous nature, which perfectly encompasses the ten directions and permeates the three periods of time;
there is no distinction between dying here and being born there, nor any differentiation between suffering for oneself and seeking happiness for others.
Because they do not awaken to this nature, they falsely cling to the view of self and stubbornly maintain their dream-like forms.
Thus they pass from suffering into suffering and from darkness into darkness, with no end in sight for their own liberation; therefore, this is called the perilous path.
Our Buddha, the Great Sage, gave rise to great compassion and, through various causes and various conditions, opened their right eye, saying: "Do not..."
Recognize this body. This body will not last long; do not crave these pleasures, for such pleasures are the cause of suffering. A hundred years are like bubbles floating upon the water;
the six sense-objects are like flashes of lightning amidst the clouds. You should recognize the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* is the very essence of one's own nature;

This is the wondrous, profound, and empty void. Holding up his *niwan* (wish-fulfilling gem), he asks: "Do you understand? If you can understand this, the ten directions will not be obstructed and the three periods of time will be harmoniously integrated.

In its greatness, it has no exterior; together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, it proclaims this with one voice. In its subtlety, it has no interior."
The patriarchs of all ages have been one in their profound stillness. If this were not so, you must examine yourself within stillness:
this body is a provisional union of four conditions; when these disperse, it has no inherent nature. This mind is a provisional spirit arising from the six sense-objects.
When they are extinguished, they originally have no self-substance. Thus, through repeated investigation and deliberation, one must ultimately discern:
"Which of these is my own self—the unborn, unceasing, eternally abiding, original face? If one practices this diligently for a long time, there will naturally come a time of arriving home.

The Buddha-eye divides its spirit into many parts. Who can directly perceive the root and foundation? How could birth and death ever be seen as constant bending and stretching?

From "I first sat at the site of enlightenment" up to "the distinct names of the Dharma and the Saṅgha," these ten lines praise the Buddha’s thoughts after he had already attained the Way— specifically, his intention as to how those who were ignorant and deluded might be delivered. Next,
from "At that time, the various Brahma kings" up to "they entreated me to turn the wheel of Dharma," these eight lines praise the [entreaties of] the various [deities].
The section on the celestial beings’ request for the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma begins with the eight lines from "I then reflected upon myself" to "quickly entered nirvana.
These verses express the sentiment that if one were to preach the wondrous Dharma, people would surely not believe it; thus, it would be better not to preach it at all.
The next section, beginning with the twenty lines from "I then recalled the Buddhas of the past" to "only to instruct the bodhisattvas," [continues this theme].

Two lines: These verses praise the Buddhas of the ten directions and express their exhortation that the Buddha, wishing to transform sentient beings, should skillfully expound the intent of the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, they cite the passage from "Śāriputra, you should know" up to "the distinct names of Dharma and Saṃgha"; these constitute eighteen lines.

This verse expresses the Great Sage Buddha’s intent in employing provisional means (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). Let us once again examine these two dharmas—provisional and real—in detail.
Now, as for "provisional" (*upāya*), it refers to skillful transformation; because it is able to reverse the conventional to accord with the Way, it is called "skillful transformation.
For example, while the ultimate essence is devoid of birth and death, the body itself undergoes birth and death; this is what the provisional teaching describes as "this body."
Before long, his life-force and light passed away. One should investigate the essence of the perfect and eternal, which is neither born nor dies;
it is like the profound stillness of ultimate reality, fundamentally devoid of right and wrong. Yet, amidst the turmoil of worldly affairs, there nevertheless appear right and wrong.
Thus, the provisional teaching says: all conditioned phenomena ultimately return to emptiness and stillness; one should investigate the vast expanse that is neither right nor wrong.
Such is its subtlety. In this way, even that which is small is taught so as to become great; that which is base is taught so as to become sublime;
that which is narrow is taught so as to become broad; and that which is suffering is taught so as to become blissful—all these are termed "expedient means" (upāya).
The "Real" refers to the Real Vehicle (*bhūta-yāna*). It is called the Real Vehicle because it is true suchness (*tathatā*) and free from delusion.
It is like the wondrous nature inherently possessed by every person: it does not shift throughout ten thousand ages, and it presides over all phenomena without distinction.

Profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; brilliant, radiant, numinous, and luminous; it neither departs nor arrives, neither arises nor ceases; it is neither great nor small, yet it is both one and myriad.
It cannot be known by intellect; it cannot be cognized by consciousness. The Great Sages, the Buddhas, realize this and call it "Perfect Equality" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Great Sages of all ages uphold this and call it the "Middle Way. The multitude are deluded by this and call it the "Sea of Birth and Death.
Those who know and clearly recognize it call it the "Pure Dharmakāya. Raising his *añjali* (hands joined), he said: "I, this mountain monk, am also [this]."
One does not know this; one does not recognize this; one is not deluded by this; nor does one realize this.
Tell me, what do you call it? *Ei!* Listen to this mountain verse: "The nature of one's own mind is known by oneself; why must the Tathāgata exert effort to uplift it?
Once he has exerted effort and uplifted it, the great thousandfold world-system shines with brilliance everywhere. He asked: "As for 'as'..."
“What is this, one’s own original nature? The Master held up his whisk and said, “Do you understand? The monk replied, “If so, then every encounter with phenomena is the truth;
there is no need for deliberation. The Master said, “The sun rises in the sky, the moon descends; before the railing, the mountains are deep and the waters are cold.
The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “What is the use of understanding? The monk said, “If that is so, then whatever is brought forth—”

"No," [the Master] said. "Do you not give rise to doubt when it is applied? The Master asked, "Do you still remember the *huatou* (critical phrase)? The monk prostrated and said, "I have received your seal of approval:
from time immemorial... (until)... all shall likewise become Buddhas."
These four lines of verse summarize the intent of employing skillful means to reveal the provisional teachings.

The phrase "Furthermore, Śāriputra, you should know" up to "this is precisely the time" constitutes twelve lines of verse, indicating that the Dharma has been preached for a long time and the minds of the assembly have become pure.
I shall now expound the sublime Dharma to reveal the meaning of this sublime nature.
Again, from "Śāriputra, you should know" up to "only teaching the unsurpassed path," these eight lines of verse describe how those of meager merit and small wisdom do not believe in this sutra.
Since such people have already regressed, [the Buddha] intends to speak with straightforwardness. From "When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma" up to "they shall all likewise become Buddhas."

These four lines of verse express the meaning that once one encounters the Tathāgata’s path of correct practice, regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Although my talent is not acute, my realization likewise has its source. Let us try once more to take up the phrase "all shall also become Buddhas" and examine it again.

Mind. This mind belongs neither to the knowing nor to the unknowing; it belongs neither to the having of marks nor to the absence of marks.

Because the Way of the past is the same, it shall remain one and the same Way from the present until ten million ages into the future.
Because the Way is the same throughout the three periods of time, the Way spoken by our Buddha, the Great Sage, is likewise...
There is no difference. Therefore, it is said that he "preaches the Dharma of non-discrimination. Holding up his *śakti* (staff), he asks: "Do you understand?

for since the establishment of heaven and earth, one does not know how many years have passed before a single Buddha appears in the world, as stated in the original [text].
In the system of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, one kalpa consists of 129,600 years;

thus, more than seventy-five thousand years have passed since the teachings of the Buddha first appeared, yet it is said that even before that time, no Buddha had been heard of. Therefore, it is said:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter. Furthermore, it was forty-two years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that [the aforementioned period] began.
He preached the Lotus Sūtra; hence it is said that the appearance of a True Teacher in the world is rare, and for him to preach this Dharma is even more difficult.
Furthermore, as for this mountain monk, he followed the cycle of samsaric cause and effect from time immemorial, unaware of its beginning.
Because he had not yet heard this wondrous Dharma, he still remained on the level of an ordinary person. Now, having encountered and heard it, and even having lectured upon this sutra—this...
Is it not difficult to hear or to preach this Sūtra? Therefore it is said: "For immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, it is difficult to hear this Dharma;

If you can realize this here and now, the Buddhas of the ten directions will all appear simultaneously to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. The Patriarchs of successive generations..."
The Master attained enlightenment all at once and transmitted the mind-seal. He unified the ancient and the modern within a single thought-moment;
every object was the pure and wondrous body. He integrated the ocean of lands into the tip of a hair; every phenomenon was the true suchness of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Should this not be so, I ask that you burn incense and sit in silence within a quiet chamber, contemplating the koan: "All phenomena return to one. After a long time...

It is inherently perfected from the beginning, lacking nothing. If you still hesitate, listen to these mountain verses:
"How could the wondrous Way ever depart from one's own mind? Moment after moment, do not seek it elsewhere. Turn the light back and directly perceive its source."

[The Master said: "A blink of an eye or a raising of an eyebrow is the Total Wondrous Sound. [The student] asked: "What is it to become 'one solid piece'? The Master said: "To be devoid of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure;
to be without intentionality, persistence, stubbornness, or selfhood. [The student] said: "If that is so, then simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Tathāgata.
The Master said: "It is like the method of smelting ore. Once the impurities of stone have been removed, the gold naturally becomes pure. [The student] said: "I am learning..."

it is truly rare among men. [The student] asked, "I often see those who recollect the Buddha at the time of death with no place to go; how is that? The Master said:

The Way is precisely the Dharma (*dharma*), which is also called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As for why the sutras say there are no *śrāvaka* disciples:
it is because a *śrāvaka* attains realization by hearing sounds, as if the Way were located elsewhere. Since the attainment of the Way...

The fish leap and the kites fly. The Master said, "Above and below are clearly manifest; inside and out are transparently penetrating.

The Dharma shatters the delusions of the five turbidities. Because those in this world of the five turbidities and evil ages are all attached to worldly desires, they ultimately fail to awaken on their own to seek the true Way of the self-nature. This true Way of the self-nature is precisely the One Buddha Vehicle;
it is also called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Indeed, this wondrous nature is inherently possessed by every person and fully realized by each individual.
It is simply because one cannot overcome the selfishness of self-grasping that one is ultimately ensnared by the marks of the self (*ātman*).
Consequently, one gradually drifts further from the entire reality of the Great Way (*mahā-mārga*), giving rise to arbitrary false views and chaotic, deviant thoughts.
Because such evil perceptions exist, the sufferings of the three realms burn fiercely, and the four marks of existence surge forth in a frantic race.

If one wishes to restore the reality of one's own nature, how could it ever be attained? Our Buddha, the Great Sage, takes the Dharma-realm as his own nature and regards all phenomena as his own body;
thus he appears in the world. Although he teaches the Three Vehicles as provisional means, he ultimately speaks for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle.
Holding up his *cintāmaṇi* jewel, he asks: "Do you understand? If, regarding this..."
You will understand. Even seeking the substantial reality of "one" is unattainable; so what need is there to speak of the four turbidities or the five turbidities?
Even seeking the substantial vehicle of "one" is unattainable; so what need is there to discuss the two vehicles or the three vehicles?
If you have not yet reached this point, you must let go further and further, sweep away further and further, and single-mindedly raise up the word "No."
When one has thoroughly mastered the practice of the "taste" of the *huatou*, awakening will inevitably occur. In dreams, the six realms of existence are vividly present;
upon waking, all is empty, and there is not even a trace of the great chiliocosm. Reaching such a state, even speaking of the three realms is like the reflection of the moon upon the water.
I shall speak of the four marks. Bird tracks in the sky—*ei*. Listen to this mountain verse: Sudden awakening to the gate of the true reality-mark;
Gate after gate, originally no walls or fences. Within the nest of right and wrong, the lotus blooms; In the arena of ordinary and sage, perfect enlightenment is pure.

This refers to that nature which is vast and boundless, whose life has neither beginning nor end, in which all virtues are perfectly complete and all principles are perfectly penetrating—the one who is originally a Buddha. Therefore, our Buddha, the Great Sage, [taught that] the four modes of birth are identical...
The essence of benevolence consists in the wisdom that recognizes the commonality of all beings; thus, it gives rise to great compassion and expounds this wondrous sutra.

Appendix: A Verse by the Tianchi Śramaṇa Faju on the Clarity of Teaching and Practice.

The clarity of teaching and practice has never been divided into two paths; Yet people arbitrarily adopt and reject, needlessly creating distinctions. The jewel in one's robes has not yet been shown to be precious.
What loss? The path by which the Treasure was personally ascended was long ago circuitous; the magpie’s cry and the elegant song reach the ultimate perfection.
Mountains bright and waters azure reveal the true form. The plucking of the flower in days of old is now fulfilled as one wishes; a single golden lotus blooms amidst the flames.
Appendix: A Poem by Chen Baisha Sent to the Venerable Taixu (other portions not fully recorded).

The Venerable Taixu dwells in a stone cave; it is solitary and remote, with few people to rely upon. A traveler from afar brought his lute to visit; having met the Master, he returned home seeking alms.
Upon the green grass sits a single rush mat; from all four sides, white clouds drift. Throughout the day there is no speech; mountain flowers fall from the crags.
Regarding the *Manyi* (Cloth-Filled) [Pagoda]: its inscription records that it was established at Baosheng Temple in Jiangdu during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty by the monk Zhidu.
During the present dynasty, as the Yangtze River waters surged and submerged [the site], Li Kai, a Commander of the Yangzhou Guard, and the monk Taixu [reconstructed it].

It was moved three *li* east of the city; it is now called Baocheng (Jewel City), though there is no historical record for this. It is suspected to be the same as Baosheng (Jewel Victorious); may you examine this further.
